name: Bagru hand block printing
summary: Bagru hand block printing is a registered Geographical Indication (2011) of Bagru and three neighbouring villages in Jaipur district, Rajasthan, practised by the hereditary Chhipa printer community using carved wooden blocks. Its classic Syahi-Begar style prints an iron 'syahi' (black) and alum 'begar' (red) mordant on harda-treated, off-white cotton and develops both colours in one alizarin/madder dyebath; its Dabu style uses a black-clay resist paste followed by indigo and yellow dyeing.

concepts.title: Bagru hand block printing
concepts.summary: Bagru Hand Block Print is mostly printed on cotton, sometimes cotton-silk, mostly with vegetable (natural) dyes, by stamping with wooden blocks.
concepts.body_md:
Bagru Hand Block Print is mostly printed on cotton, sometimes cotton-silk, mostly with vegetable (natural) dyes, by stamping with wooden blocks. [S1]

The skill of production is described as confined to the Chhipa community of Bagru, with blocks made by turners locally called Kharadiyas. [S1, S9]

Bagru printing follows two styles, direct and resist; the resist style is called Dabu. [S4]

Traditional Bagru prints are two-colour, red and black, on an off-white ground; a retailer blog describes this Bagru style as Syahi-Begar (black syahi, red begar). [S1, S7]

Bagru Hand Block Print is a registered GI (application 183, certificate 150 dated 11-05-2011). [S2]

concepts.title: The Chhipa printer-dyer community of Bagru
concepts.summary: The hand printers, known as Chhipa, migrated to Bagru from Sawai Madhopur, Alwar, Jhunjhunu and Sikar districts some 300 years ago, according to the GI dossier citing Mohanty & Mohanty (1983).
concepts.body_md:
The hand printers, known as Chhipa, migrated to Bagru from Sawai Madhopur, Alwar, Jhunjhunu and Sikar districts some 300 years ago, according to the GI dossier citing Mohanty & Mohanty (1983). [S1]

By legend, two Chhipa families were first brought by the Thakur of Bagru from Isarda village; more families followed. [S1, S4]

Bagru Chhipas claim to be descendants of Saint Namdeo of Maharashtra and fall in the Other Backward Castes category. [S5]

The Chhipas work in the Chhipa Mohalla (printers' quarter) by the Sanjaria riverside. [S4, S5]

Survey respondents in Bagru were mostly from the Khatri or Chhipa community and mostly did job-work for retailers or wholesalers. [S3]

concepts.title: Historical records of Bagru as a printing centre
concepts.summary: The Imperial Gazetteer of India (Rajputana, 1908) is cited as describing Bagru as famous for dyed and stamped chintzes.
concepts.body_md:
The Imperial Gazetteer of India (Rajputana, 1908) is cited as describing Bagru as famous for dyed and stamped chintzes. [S1]

The GI dossier describes Bagru as an early 16th-century town that became a textile production centre and peaked in the 19th century. [S1]

A Calico Museum study (Mohanty & Mohanty, 1983) documented block printing and dyeing at Bagru. [S12, S1]

A mid-to-late 19th-century block-printed, mud-resist, mordant-dyed cotton textile from Bagru, described by the Penn Museum as "for Kagra, to be worn only by a woman", is held by the Penn Museum. [S10]

A block-printed plain-weave cotton sari from Bagru, dated to the first half of the 20th century, is in the Honolulu Museum of Art (accession 3967.1). [S13]

concepts.title: Caste- and community-specific clientele
concepts.summary: Bagru prints are described as rooted in the local folk milieu, with a limited design and colour range tied to traditional caste- and custom-bound end uses.
concepts.body_md:
Bagru prints are described as rooted in the local folk milieu, with a limited design and colour range tied to traditional caste- and custom-bound end uses. [S1]

Colours and designs of Bagru prints are said to enable identification of the user community (Jat, Meena, Rajput, Mali). [S1]

Traditional goods listed include fadat (women's skirts), lugdi, dhabli, angochha, tehmat, janani dhoti, chadara and jajam. [S1]

concepts.title: Market change, synthetic dyes and screen-print imitation
concepts.summary: Fake screen-printed Bagru textiles were being sold all over India under the Bagru name, motivating GI registration.
concepts.body_md:
Fake screen-printed Bagru textiles were being sold all over India under the Bagru name, motivating GI registration. [S1]

Craftspeople in Bagru and Sanganer have adopted cheaper raw materials, including abundant chemical dyes, using natural dyes only for specific orders. [S3]

94% of surveyed Bagru units did not use the GI tag as a marketing tool. [S3]

Opening of an industrial park led artisans in the original Bagru village to lose potential customers. [S3]

Synthetic (azo-free) dyes and synthetic alizarin and indigo are used when natural dyes are unavailable. [S1]

concepts.title: Cotton cloth (latha, mulmul, handloom)
concepts.summary: Bagru goods use mill-made or handloom latha, grey superfine mulmul, cambric and rezi cloth depending on the item.
concepts.body_md:
Bagru goods use mill-made or handloom latha, grey superfine mulmul, cambric and rezi cloth depending on the item. [S1]

Fabrics include natural fibres such as cotton, cotton-silk and wool, and man-made rayon. [S1]

concepts.title: Harda (myrobalan, Terminalia chebula)
concepts.summary: Washed fabric is treated with myrobalan (harda), which contains tannic acid that attracts the mordants applied by block.
concepts.body_md:
Washed fabric is treated with myrobalan (harda), which contains tannic acid that attracts the mordants applied by block. [S1]

Harda is considered the most important element of Bagru printing and dyeing; its tannic acid acts as a mordant for the iron of the printing colour, forming Bagru black. [S4]

After harda treatment the fabric has a yellowish tint that later disappears on washing. [S5]

concepts.title: Syahi (fermented iron black)
concepts.summary: Syahi is essentially a fermented solution of iron with molasses (jaggery, gur) and gum; with harda it develops a deep black.
concepts.body_md:
Syahi is essentially a fermented solution of iron with molasses (jaggery, gur) and gum; with harda it develops a deep black. [S1]

Syahi is traditionally made by reaction of old rusted horseshoe nails with jaggery. [S1]

Black syahi is a fermented solution of iron, molasses, gum and tamarind starch that turns black on harda-treated fabric when exposed to air. [S4]

Black dye is made from rusted horseshoes left to ferment for periods of months. [S5]

concepts.title: Begar (alum mordant paste for red)
concepts.summary: Begar paste is the mordant alum which in combination with alizarin develops a rich red colour.
concepts.body_md:
Begar paste is the mordant alum which in combination with alizarin develops a rich red colour. [S1]

For the red outline, alum, geru and natural gum are mixed with water into a paste, with ghee and oil added when foam forms. [S4]

Reds (begar) are made by mixing alum (fitkari), madder and babul gum in varying proportions. [S6, S7]

Red is described as a mixture of natural gum paste, pieces of rust and alum. [S5]

concepts.title: Madder / alizarin dyebath
concepts.summary: The red dyebath uses madder (Rubia tinctorum, Rubia manjista), which contains alizarin and purpurin; synthetic alizarin is now used due to shortage.
concepts.body_md:
The red dyebath uses madder (Rubia tinctorum, Rubia manjista), which contains alizarin and purpurin; synthetic alizarin is now used due to shortage. [S1]

Alizarin is used as the dye throughout Rajasthan, giving red with alum and black with ferrous mordant. [S1]

concepts.summary: Dhawai flower (Woodfordia floribunda) is boiled along with alizarin to avoid patches and staining.
concepts.body_md:
Dhawai flower (Woodfordia floribunda) is boiled along with alizarin to avoid patches and staining. [S1]

Red-printed fabric is boiled in a copper vessel with dhaura flowers and a few drops of castor or sesame oil. [S7]

concepts.title: Bagru dabu (black-clay resist paste)
concepts.summary: Dabu paste is prepared by mixing kali mitti (clay soil), lime, wheat flour and gum in ratios depending on the type of dabu needed.
concepts.body_md:
Dabu paste is prepared by mixing kali mitti (clay soil), lime, wheat flour and gum in ratios depending on the type of dabu needed. [S1]

The dabu used at Bagru is made of locally available black clay soil. [S1]

Dabu is lime dissolved in water, natural gum 'bedhan' or wheat flour spoiled by worms, and local black clay, mashed and left overnight, then strained. [S4]

The art of making dabu paste is kept secret and every family has its own recipe. [S1, S4]

Dabu resist paste is made from local black clay (kaali mitti), wheat powder, guar gum and lime water. [S6]

concepts.summary: Sawdust absorbs water from the dabu paste and gives an additional layer of resist.
concepts.body_md:
Sawdust absorbs water from the dabu paste and gives an additional layer of resist. [S1]

Sawdust is sprinkled before the prints dry completely to avoid the cloth sticking to itself. [S4, S6]

concepts.title: Indigo (neel)
concepts.summary: Indigo blue (nil) is extracted from Indigofera tinctoria; synthetic indigo granules are also used nowadays.
concepts.body_md:
Indigo blue (nil) is extracted from Indigofera tinctoria; synthetic indigo granules are also used nowadays. [S1]

Once ready, an indigo vat is kept alive by constant addition of indigo, lime and jaggery. [S1]

Natural indigo is boiled with pawar seeds, kept overnight, then dissolved with lime in vats about 15 feet deep. [S4]

concepts.title: Alum (fitkari)
concepts.summary: Post-mordanting with diluted alum (fitkari) in a big copper vessel makes the yellow dye fast.
concepts.body_md:
Post-mordanting with diluted alum (fitkari) in a big copper vessel makes the yellow dye fast. [S1]

Alum solution fixes colour and also helps remove the dabu paste; its quantity varies with the strength of the dabu. [S4]

concepts.summary: Traditionally cow dung was used for scouring; soaps have now replaced it.
concepts.body_md:
Traditionally cow dung was used for scouring; soaps have now replaced it. [S1, S5]

Telkhar emulsion is used for oiling and alkaline treatment to desize and partially bleach grey cloth. [S1]

A paste of cow dung, soda ash and sesame oil is prepared over two days to wash the cloth. [S4]

concepts.title: Wooden printing block (bunta) — gadh, rekh, datta
concepts.summary: Buntas are wooden hand-printing blocks of different shapes with motifs engraved on the bottom face and a wooden handle; the GI names the outline block (rekh) and filler block (dotu), and a maker profile names the background (gudh), outline (rekh) and filler (datta) blocks.
concepts.body_md:
Buntas are wooden hand-printing blocks of different shapes with motifs engraved on the bottom face and a wooden handle; the GI names the outline block (rekh) and filler block (dotu), and a maker profile names the background (gudh), outline (rekh) and filler (datta) blocks. [S1, S6]

The outline block is called rekh, the background block gadh, and the colour-filling block datta. [S5, S6]

Blocks are soaked in oil for about 10-15 days after making; their life is about 600-800 m of printing. [S5]

Blocks are soaked overnight in mustard or refined oil and washed before printing. [S4]

Carvers use teak for durability, sheesham for intricate detail, and also rohida; carving one block can take one to two days. [S6]

concepts.summary: Pathiya is a low table used for dabu printing, mostly by older printers and women who cannot stand long; mej is a long table for regular production.

The printing table is covered with canvas and jute. [S5]

Grey cotton is the input cloth.
Repeated wetting and sun-drying until the cloth becomes white is a sun/moisture bleaching practice.
relationships.conditions: Source describes the practice, not the mechanism.

relationships.explanation: Cloth is spread on open ground and re-wetted for 3-6 days.
Cloth is soaked in harda solution.
Dried harda cloth is beaten with a wooden mallet.
Harda's tannic acid attracts the mordants applied afterwards.
Harda gives the yellowish/cream ground distinguishing Bagru from Sanganer.
relationships.conditions: Gaatha reports the yellow tint later washes out.

relationships.explanation: Syahi is printed, usually with the outline block.
Begar is printed with the filler block.
Patterns are stamped with carved wooden blocks.
Cloth is spread on a padded table.
The block is charged from a padded colour tray.
Block order and registration are decided during printing.
Because syahi shows black immediately on harda cloth, the outline can guide placement of the filler block.
Iron–tannin complex formation explains the syahi black.
Syahi develops black in combination with harda.
Printed cloth is dried/aged, in the sun per some accounts.
Washing in running water is required.
Alizarin/madder is the dye.
Dhawai flowers are boiled with alizarin.
Dyeing is done in wood-fired copper vessels.
The dyer judges alizarin quantity.
One bath reacts with two printed mordants.
Metal–alizarin lake formation underlies the red and black.
Aluminium from begar complexes alizarin to give red.
Red on begar areas and black on syahi areas.
Dabu paste is block-printed.
Sawdust is sprinkled on wet dabu.
The low pathiya table is used mainly for dabu printing.
Dabu-printed cloth is dried in the sun before indigo.
Recipe ratios are chosen by type of dabu required.
Dabu works as a mechanical barrier to dye.
Generic mud-resist barrier mechanism.
Indigo vat dyeing.
Cloth is lowered into deep vats.
Vat state is judged by colour during indigo work.
Pleats are opened under the liquor and handled gently.
Colour develops as reduced indigo oxidises in air.
Vat reduction / re-oxidation chemistry of indigo.
Resisted areas remain light against indigo.
relationships.conditions: After final washing removes the dabu.

relationships.explanation: Turmeric-pomegranate yellow is sponged on.
Dabu is re-printed to keep some blue areas.
Dilute alum bath.
Dip time is kept short so dabu does not come off.
Alum makes the fugitive yellow fast.
Aluminium–dye complexation.
Fixed yellow over indigo gives green.
Cloth is beaten (on stone) to remove resist and loose dye.
Beating is done where water flows.
Washing generates effluent (GI dossier: aerated before discharge); Gaatha reports chemicals in the water seeping underground. No source directly measures final-washing effluent as the cause.
Chhipas are the practising community.
Kharadis carve the blocks.
Chisels engrave the motifs.
Settlement is attributed to abundant water and the river bed.
Defines the protected area.
Historical evidence of the tradition.
Limited palette tied to caste- and custom-bound end uses.
Imitations and dye substitution pressure the craft.
The syahi-begar print realises the red-black palette.
Each layer needs its own block.
Defines the motif vocabulary in the GI specification.
A falling water table threatens production.
Ground colour is the main stated visual difference.
The settlement date of the Chhipas is disputed.
Records the conflicting begar recipes.
Flags the untested water-quality claims.
A design observation about Bagru printing: open modern layouts expose dye drips.
Production follows the seasons: cloth is dried in courtyards in the hot dry months, and the monsoon halts work (S6).
